Q: Exception while connecting to DB2 in java using JDBC A:

Your first two attempts were not supposed to work. You're using the JCC driver URL format, so it wouldn't be valid for either "net" or "app" drivers, which are deprecated anyway.

Use the JCC driver (com.ibm.db2.jcc.DB2Driver) and the URL format of "jdbc:db2://hostname:portnumber/databasename" and see this technote for the solution to the "Security mechanism not supported" problem. In short, you need to use a supported JDK.

Q: SEVERE: Exception sending context initialized event to listener A:

On the Tomcat server is probably deployed some Web application which uses Spring framework. In configuration of this Spring framework is referenced property file:

\opt\tej2\resources\config\db.properties

but this file is probably missing so Spring framework fails to initialize.

Nevertheless Tomcat server should be running OK. Only particular Web application with spring framework failed to start up.

Q: Inject Custom Variable into ngx_http_fastcgi_module at Runtime from a Third-Party Module A:

No, not for arbitrary FastCGI param names at pure request runtime.

"ngx_http_fastcgi_module" builds the FastCGI PARAMS record inside

"ngx_http_fastcgi_create_request()".

If the param name is not already known by the FastCGI module, another third-party module cannot cleanly add this at runtime: MY_VAR=hello, without patching or replacing the ngx_http_fastcgi_module.c.

There are two practical alternatives.

1. Use r->headers_in for HTTP_* params

In ngx_http_fastcgi_module.c, notice the function:

ngx_http_fastcgi_create_request()

Inside that function, NGINX reads request headers from:

r->headers_in

and converts them into FastCGI params using this pattern:

HTTP_ + uppercase(header name, with "-" changed to "_")

For example:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer testtoken123" http://example.com/

can be visible in PHP as:

$_SERVER["HTTP_AUTHORIZATION"]

because FastCGI converts request headers like this:

Authorization -> HTTP_AUTHORIZATION
X-My-Var      -> HTTP_X_MY_VAR
User-Agent    -> HTTP_USER_AGENT

So a third-party module can add or modify request headers before ngx_http_fastcgi_create_request() runs.

The limitation is that this only gives HTTP_* params, not arbitrary names like MY_VAR.

2. Use a generated include with dynamic NGINX variable values

Keep one static include in nginx.conf:

location ~ \.php$ {
    fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php-fpm.sock;
    include /path/generated_fastcgi_params.conf;
}

Generate that file automatically:

fastcgi_param MY_VAR $my_var;
fastcgi_param APP_ENV $app_env;

Then your module can set the value of $my_var and $app_env dynamically at request runtime.

So the final rule is:

FastCGI param names must exist before ngx_http_fastcgi_create_request() runs.
FastCGI param values can be dynamic set in run time handler.

This allows behavior similar to Apache mod_env / SetEnv, without patching
ngx_http_fastcgi_module, but new param names require to be set first in include file in nginx.conf , you can inject that in config time dynamically via preconfiguration from conf buffer,etc

Q: Why does this C program compile despite apparently defining a local function without a return type? A:

foo is declared as a function local to main function

Not true. It declares but does not define that a function foo exists, and that it takes an unknown number of arguments and returns a struct date.

This declaration is compatible with the actual definition of foo, as the return types match and the declaration makes no statement about the arguments.

Q: Always best to use float in python script instead of int? A:

tl;dr: int and float are different; don't confuse the one for the other.

Python integers have a super-power: they are much more expressive than floats. Python floats have a super-power: they can express concepts like "one half" or "one eighth" which an int cannot.

There's at most 2 ** 64 distinct double precision floats, with many of the bit patterns corresponding to other things like NaN's. Here is one float:

denom = 2 ** 55
x = .1
y = 3_602_879_701_896_397 / denom
print(x == y, f"\n{x.hex()=}\n{x.as_integer_ratio()=}")

True 
x.hex()='0x1.999999999999ap-4'
x.as_integer_ratio()=(3602879701896397, 36028797018963968)

Notice that we cannot exactly represent the notion of one-tenth using a single float. There are lots of float values; there's just a finite amount of distinct floats so they can't represent everything on the number line. (Base ten is odd, so that factor of five throws a monkey wrench into the works when denominator must be a power of two. The literal .1 gets turned into the closest ratio available. It's a bit like representing one-third, .3333, as a repeating decimal.)

A float data structure is a fair model of a mathematician's real number line, but it discretizes the number line and can only represent a finite subset of it.

Now let's compute powers of two.

>>> n = 1
>>> for i in range(500):
...     print(f"{i:4}   {n}")
...     n *= 2
...     
   0   1
   1   2
   2   4
   3   8
   4   16
   5   32
   ...
 499   1636695303948070935006594848413799576108321023021532394741645684048066898202337277441635046162952078575443342063780035504608628272942696526664263794688

Try that in most languages and you'll run out of steam when you get to 64 bits, and will need to import some BigNum library. Python doesn't bat an eyelash, it just keeps allocating more storage -- at least 500 bits, in this example.

An int data structure exactly corresponds to a mathematician's notion of integers. Well, a mathematician can readily talk about limits and various kinds of infinities, while python is restricted to representing specific integers. But, if you can write an integer down, python is happy to store an exact representation of it for you!

Now let's try passing in a float where an int was expected.

>>> a = list(range(6))
>>> a[2]
2
>>> a[2.0]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-14>", line 1, in <module>
    a[2.0]
    ~^^^^^
TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not float
>>> 
>>> range(6.0)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-16>", line 1, in <module>
    range(6.0)
    ~~~~~^^^^^
TypeError: 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
>>>

Let's take a peek over in JavaScript land, where famously an integer literal like 2 is represented as a float value.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Number/MAX_SAFE_INTEGER

The Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER static data property represents the maximum safe integer in JavaScript (2^53 – 1).

That's because IEEE allocated 53 bits of significand in its double precision specification.

if I always use float I won't have to worry later on when a decimal number input comes

Yes, and no. Those two types are different things, with very different abilities. If you're counting years (or even seconds) since a certain cuneiform document was written, then yes, they're pretty much interchangeable. But each has its uniquely helpful abilities, and you'll want to use the right type in the right situation.

Q: oauth2-proxy with Keycloak and ingress-nginx returns "csrf cookie not found" after successful authentication A:

I think the problem might be oauth2-proxy session cookie can't reach fastapi.test, because auth.test and fastapi.test have no shared cookieable parent domain.

Below is what you can try I believe. a shared parent domain

For one session cookie to be sent to both the auth host and each protected app, the cookie's Domain attribute has to be a parent of both. .test is a reserved TLD and is treated as a public suffix by browsers, they will refuse to set a cookie on it. So auth.test and fastapi.test have no usable shared parent, and no amount of oauth2-proxy or nginx config will make the centralized pattern work as-is**.**

Move everything under one extra label, e.g. app.test:

127.0.0.1 fastapi.app.test
127.0.0.1 auth.app.test
127.0.0.1 keycloak.app.test

Then tell oauth2-proxy to set its cookies on the parent and to allow rd= redirects within it:

extraArgs:
  provider: oidc
  oidc-issuer-url: https://keycloak.app.test/realms/zero-trust-local-platform
  redirect-url:   https://auth.app.test/oauth2/callback

  cookie-domain:    ".app.test"     # session + CSRF cookies scoped to the parent
  whitelist-domain: ".app.test"     # allow rd= to any subdomain under it
  cookie-secure:    "true"
  cookie-samesite:  "lax"           # 'strict' breaks the callback; 'lax' is correct here

  email-domain: "*"
  skip-provider-button: true
  reverse-proxy: "true"
  set-authorization-header: "true"
  set-xauthrequest: "true"
  pass-access-token: "true"
  pass-user-headers: "true"

We will have to make sure to match the new names

  • the three Ingress host: entries and their TLS cert SANs,

  • hostAliases in the oauth2-proxy Deployment,

  • the Keycloak client's Valid Redirect URIs (https://auth.app.test/oauth2/callback) and Web Origins,

  • the auth-signin annotation on each protected Ingress, which should now read:

  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-url:    "https://auth.app.test/oauth2/auth"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-signin: "https://auth.app.test/oauth2/start?rd=$scheme://$host$request_uri"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-response-headers: "Authorization,X-Auth-Request-User,X-Auth-Request-Email,X-Auth-Request-Access-Token"

Using the external auth.app.test URL for auth-url (instead of the in-cluster Service DNS) is recommended in the oauth2-proxy + nginx-ingress docs precisely because it makes nginx forward the browser's cookies to the auth check on the right host which is the whole point once the cookie is on .app.test.

Once that's in place, the cookie set on .app.test during the callback is sent on the next request to fastapi.app.test, the auth_request subrequest returns 200, and the loop stops. You can then add app1.app.test, app2.app.test, etc., with no extra oauth2-proxy changes that's the centralized pattern you sketched.

Above answer I have not tried but it might be the direction I believe.
